item.title: Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast
item.description:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States is again fighting a major war in the Middle East. Drop Site’s Ryan Grim and Murtaza Hussain speak with Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at Johns Hopkins SAIS and a former senior adviser in the Obama administration, and Rob Malley, a senior fellow at Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs, former U.S. special envoy for Iran, longtime Middle East peace negotiator, and head of the Middle East program at the International Crisis Group. The conversation covers Ansarallah’s advance in Yemen, the battle over the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and the US duel strategies of economic pressure, the future of U.S. military bases in the Gulf, the collapse of the JCPOA, Iran’s nuclear calculations, and whether Washington has learned the lessons of Iraq, Afghanistan and the broader post-9/11 wars. item.title: Federal court rejects Trump administration order keeping Michigan coal plant open
item.description:
The Department of Energy overstepped when it ordered an aging coal-fired power plant in Michigan to stay open past its planned retirement date last year, a federal court ruled on Friday. The J.H Campbell plant is one of seven fossil fuel plants around the country that the Trump administration has forced to stay in operation, despite the pollution they cause and the enormous costs of keeping them online. Just before it was about to close last May, Trump’s Energy Department invoked short-term emergency powers under the Federal Power Act to keep the 64-year-old plant running, arguing that the threat of outages, along with the need for more energy to power data centers, constituted an emergency. item.description:

September 11 was an epochal break, the violent punctuation mark with which one era ended and another began. We have stories on how it changed the world, the war on terror that followed, its contested legacy today, and more. item.title: Jimmy Kimmel Didn't Air Talarico Interview Over Fear of FCC 'Equal Time' Threats
item.description:
For the second time this year, James Talarico, the Texas Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, appeared on a late-night talk show only to get bumped from the nightly broadcast. In each case, both the hosts and the network seemingly buckled to pressure from President Donald Trump and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). And just like in that earlier case, it provides a perfect example of why we should abolish the equal time rule. "I'll be interviewing James Talarico tomorrow night under unusual circumstances," Jimmy Kimmel said Wednesday on his ABC talk show. But the TV audience would not see the segment because of fears that by airing it, ABC's affiliates could run afoul of the equal opportunities requirement , better known as the equal time rule. item.title: ‘War on terror’: How 9/11 changed the language of conflict
item.description:
The first murder I witnessed was at age 3, on September 11, 2001. Although I was too young to fully grasp what the burning towers across the Hudson River meant, I soon came to understand that many families around us had lost someone forever. (I later learned that, like many other New Yorkers, my aunt barely missed becoming one of the victims by being late to work.) And I heard that a stranger from a strange land named "Osama bin Laden" was responsible. A little under a decade later, the U.S. government announced that it had killed bin Laden, to the jubilation of my middle school classmates. But the end of bin Laden did not bring the relief that Americans were hoping for. President Barack Obama was quick to warn the public that "his death does not mark the end of our effort."
